docs.x: Louisiana appellate deadline. Supreme Court certiorari: 30 days from Transmission of the court of appeal’s notice of judgment, or of notice of denial of rehearing (La. C.C.P. art. 2166(A)–(C)). Second applicant: later of 30 days or 10 days after notice of the first application.

docs.t: Louisiana appeal deadline — Opposition to Supreme Court writ application
docs.x: Louisiana appellate deadline. Opposition to Supreme Court writ application: 30 days from Date of the Court’s acknowledgment letter (La. Sup. Ct. R. X, § 5). No extensions absent clear and convincing proof of circumstances beyond the party’s control.

docs.t: Louisiana appeal deadline — Supreme Court rehearing
docs.x: Louisiana appellate deadline. Supreme Court rehearing: 14 days from Transmission of notice of judgment (La. C.C.P. art. 2167(A)). Only after a grant of writ, appeal, or other proceeding.

docs.t: Louisiana appeal deadline — City or parish court appeal
docs.x: Louisiana appellate deadline. City or parish court appeal: 10 days from Judgment, or service of notice of judgment when required (La. C.C.P. art. 5002). To the court of appeal.

docs.t: Louisiana appeal deadline — Suspensive appeal from eviction
docs.x: Louisiana appellate deadline. Suspensive appeal from eviction: 1 days from Rendition of judgment of eviction (La. C.C.P. art. 4735). 24 hours; also requires a sworn answer pleading an affirmative defense.

docs.t: Maryland — The Maryland Rules, not the Federal Rules
docs.x: Maryland land mine. The Maryland Rules, not the Federal Rules: Circuit court civil practice is under Title 2 of the Maryland Rules, District Court practice under Title 3, and appeals under Title 8. Their numbering and deadlines differ from the federal rules. These rules have the force of law. (Rule text was not collected for this page; read the current Rules.) (Md. Const. art. IV, § 18(a); Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 1-201)

docs.t: Maryland — Two different trial courts, and the $5,000 / $30,000 lines
docs.x: Maryland land mine. Two different trial courts, and the $5,000 / $30,000 lines: The District Court has exclusive jurisdiction over contract and tort claims up to $30,000 and over small claims up to $5,000. Above $5,000 (except replevin, landlord-tenant and certain other cases) the plaintiff may choose the District Court or the circuit court. Claims for equity relief (outside the listed exceptions), title to real property, and declaratory judgments must go to the circuit court. The $30,000 cap changes under laws effective June 30, 2028 and 2029; check the version in effect. (Cts. & Jud. Proc. §§ 4-401(1), 4-402(a)-(d), 4-405)

docs.t: Maryland — District Court appeal: 30 days, filed in the District Court, often de novo
docs.x: Maryland land mine. District Court appeal: 30 days, filed in the District Court, often de novo: Appeals from District Court civil judgments go to the circuit court for the same county (or Baltimore City), not to the Appellate Court. File the order for appeal with the District Court clerk within 30 days of the final judgment; certain landlord-tenant cases have shorter, section-specific times. If more than $5,000 is in controversy (excluding interest, costs and recoverable fees), or the parties agree, the appeal is on the record. Otherwise it is tried de novo. (Cts. & Jud. Proc. §§ 12-401(a), (e), (f), 12-403)

docs.t: Maryland — No further appeal of right after the circuit court reviews the District Court
docs.x: Maryland land mine. No further appeal of right after the circuit court reviews the District Court: A circuit court judgment entered in its appellate capacity (reviewing the District Court, an agency or a local legislative body) cannot be appealed under § 12-301 unless a statute expressly grants the right. The only route is a petition for certiorari to the Supreme Court of Maryland, granted for uniformity of decision or special public-interest circumstances. (Cts. & Jud. Proc. §§ 12-302(a), 12-305)

docs.t: Maryland — Interlocutory appeals are a closed statutory list
docs.x: Maryland land mine. Interlocutory appeals are a closed statutory list: Civil interlocutory appeals lie only from the orders listed in § 12-303. Examples: possession of property; injunctions (an appeal from granting an injunction, refusing to dissolve one, or appointing a receiver requires the appellant to have filed an answer first); orders for payment of money or sale of property; certain custody orders; and orders staying arbitration. Denial of an anti-SLAPP motion is not on the list. (Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 12-303(3)(i), (ii), (iv), (v), (ix), (x))

docs.t: Maryland — Anti-SLAPP is weak: bad faith required, no fees, no deadline
docs.x: Maryland land mine. Anti-SLAPP is weak: bad faith required, no fees, no deadline: Unlike many states’ statutes, § 5-807 requires the plaintiff to have sued in bad faith and with intent to inhibit, or with the effect of inhibiting, protected rights. It provides only a hearing ‘as soon as practicable’ or a stay. There is no fee award and no automatic discovery stay. (Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 5-807(b), (d))

docs.t: Maryland — Venue: negligence torts may be filed where the claim arose; nonresident defendants anywhere
docs.x: Maryland land mine. Venue: negligence torts may be filed where the claim arose; nonresident defendants anywhere: General venue is where a defendant resides, carries on regular business, is employed or habitually works (and for a corporation, also its principal Maryland office). A negligence tort may also be brought where it arose. A damages action against a nonresident individual may be brought in any county. With several defendants and no common venue, sue where any defendant could be sued or where the claim arose. (Cts. & Jud. Proc. §§ 6-201, 6-202(8), (11))

docs.t: Maryland — Three-year default limitations period
docs.x: Maryland land mine. Three-year default limitations period: A civil action at law must be filed within three years from accrual unless another Code provision sets a different period. (Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 5-101)

docs.t: Maryland — Supreme Court review is by certiorari, and some leave denials are final
docs.x: Maryland land mine. Supreme Court review is by certiorari, and some leave denials are final: Review of Appellate Court cases is by petition for certiorari, which may be filed before or after the Appellate Court decides, within the time set by the Maryland Rules. The writ issues if review is ‘desirable and in the public interest.’ Certiorari is barred where the Appellate Court granted or denied leave to appeal in categories listed in § 12-202, such as guilty-plea judgments and probation revocations. (Cts. & Jud. Proc. §§ 12-201, 12-202, 12-203)

docs.t: Maryland — Pro hac vice and professional conduct rules are not on this page
docs.x: Maryland land mine. Pro hac vice and professional conduct rules are not on this page: Rule 19-217 (pro hac vice) and the Maryland Attorneys’ Rules of Professional Conduct could not be collected (mdcourts.gov bot block). Read them directly before appearing; do not rely on another state’s practice for the sponsor, fee, or numerical limits. (Md. Rules 19-217, 19-300.1 ff. (not verified))

docs.t: Maryland anti-SLAPP — Statute: Courts & Judicial Proceedings § 5-807
docs.x: Maryland anti-SLAPP. Statute: Courts & Judicial Proceedings § 5-807: A suit is a SLAPP suit only if all three elements are met: (1) it is brought in bad faith against a party who communicated with a federal, State or local government body or the public at large on a matter within a government body’s authority or an issue of public concern, exercising rights under the First Amendment or Articles 10, 13 or 40 of the Maryland Declaration of Rights; (2) it is materially related to that communication; and (3) it is intended to inhibit, or does inhibit, those rights. A SLAPP defendant who acted without constitutional malice is not civilly liable for the communication. (Md. Code, Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 5-807(a)-(c))

docs.t: Maryland anti-SLAPP — Procedure: motion to dismiss or stay; no stated deadline
docs.x: Maryland anti-SLAPP. Procedure: motion to dismiss or stay; no stated deadline: The defendant may move to (1) dismiss, and the court must hold a hearing ‘as soon as practicable’; or (2) stay all court proceedings until the underlying matter the defendant communicated about is resolved. The statute sets no filing deadline, no discovery stay, no evidentiary burden-shifting, and no time limit for the ruling. It applies notwithstanding any other law or rule, and it preserves every other legal or equitable remedy. (Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 5-807(d)-(e))

docs.t: Maryland anti-SLAPP — No fee-shifting and no special appeal right
docs.x: Maryland anti-SLAPP. No fee-shifting and no special appeal right: Section 5-807 contains no attorney’s fee or cost award. It does not create an immediate appeal from denial of the motion, and denial of a § 5-807 motion is not among the interlocutory orders listed as appealable in CJ § 12-303. Whether any other route to early review exists (for example, the collateral order doctrine) was not checked; the case law was not collected. (Cts. & Jud. Proc. §§ 5-807, 12-303)

docs.t: Maryland appeal deadline — Notice of appeal from a circuit court final judgment
docs.x: Maryland appellate deadline. Notice of appeal from a circuit court final judgment: 30 days from Entry of the judgment or order appealed from (Md. Rule 8-202(a) (not verified)). NOT VERIFIED: rule text not collected (mdcourts.gov blocked). The 30-day period is the commonly cited rule; confirm it and the tolling effect of timely post-judgment motions in the current Rule 8-202.

docs.t: Maryland appeal deadline — Civil appeal from the District Court to the circuit court
docs.x: Maryland appellate deadline. Civil appeal from the District Court to the circuit court: 30 days from Date of the District Court final judgment (Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 12-401(e)(1)). File the order for appeal with the District Court clerk. Certain landlord-tenant judgments (Real Prop. §§ 8-332, 8-401, 8-402, 14-109, 14-120) have their own times.

docs.t: Maryland appeal deadline — State’s pretrial appeal from suppression or return-of-property ruling (criminal)
docs.x: Maryland appellate deadline. State’s pretrial appeal from suppression or return-of-property ruling (criminal): 15 days from Date the trial court decision is rendered (Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 12-302(c)(4)(iii)). Only in the case types listed in § 12-302(c)(4)(i), and before jeopardy attaches. The appellate decision is due within 120 days after the record is filed, or the trial ruling becomes final.

docs.t: Michigan — 21 days to appeal, and it is jurisdictional
docs.x: Michigan land mine. 21 days to appeal, and it is jurisdictional: A civil appeal of right must be filed within 21 days after entry of the judgment or order, not 30. Only a postjudgment motion for new trial, rehearing, reconsideration, or other relief filed within that initial 21-day period (or extra time the trial court allows within it) restarts the clock. After that, only a delayed application for leave (within 6 months) is available, and it is discretionary. (MCR 7.204(A)(1); MCR 7.205(A)(4))

docs.t: Michigan — Summons expires in 91 days and the case dismisses itself
docs.x: Michigan land mine. Summons expires in 91 days and the case dismisses itself: A summons expires 91 days after issuance. Unserved defendants are dismissed without prejudice automatically, with no court order needed. To extend, get a second summons by court order within the 91 days, showing due diligence; the extension may not run beyond 1 year from the original issuance. (MCR 2.102(D)–(E))

docs.t: Michigan — Personal-jurisdiction and service defenses die with your first filing
docs.x: Michigan land mine. Personal-jurisdiction and service defenses die with your first filing: Lack of personal jurisdiction and insufficient process or service must be raised in your first motion under MCR 2.116 or your responsive pleading, whichever is filed first, or they are waived. Release, statute of limitations, statute of frauds, and arbitration-agreement defenses ((C)(7)) must be in the responsive pleading or an earlier motion. (MCR 2.116(D)(1)–(2))

docs.t: Michigan — Rejecting an offer of judgment can cost you the other side’s attorney fees
docs.x: Michigan land mine. Rejecting an offer of judgment can cost you the other side’s attorney fees: Unlike Fed. R. Civ. P. 68, any party can make an offer, and the sanction includes a reasonable attorney fee from rejection forward. Failing to accept within 21 days is a rejection. Do the adjusted-verdict math before letting an offer lapse. (MCR 2.405(B)–(D))

docs.t: Michigan — Motion papers: 20 pages combined, no reply brief without permission
docs.x: Michigan land mine. Motion papers: 20 pages combined, no reply brief without permission: A motion and its brief together, or a response and its brief, may not exceed 20 double-spaced pages, and reply or supplemental briefs are barred unless the court permits. Default timing: serve a motion at least 9 days before the hearing by mail (7 by delivery) and file at least 7 days before. Serve a response at least 5 days before by mail (3 by delivery) and file at least 3 days before. Check local and judge practice, and summary disposition has its own longer schedule. (MCR 2.119(A)(2), (C); MCR 2.116(G)(1))

docs.t: Michigan — Reconsideration in 21 days, and only for ‘palpable error’
docs.x: Michigan land mine. Reconsideration in 21 days, and only for ‘palpable error’: A motion for rehearing or reconsideration is due within 21 days after the order. It gets no response or argument unless ordered, and it must show a palpable error that misled the court and parties and would change the result. Rearguing the same issues fails. (MCR 2.119(F))

docs.t: Michigan — The ‘7-day rule’ for proposed orders
docs.x: Michigan land mine. The ‘7-day rule’ for proposed orders: If an order is not entered at the hearing, a party may serve a proposed order with notice that it will be submitted for signature unless written objections are filed within 7 days. Ignore it and the order enters as drafted. The party who obtains a signed judgment or order must serve it on all parties within 7 days. (MCR 2.602(B)(3), (E)(1))

docs.t: Michigan — Interrogatories capped at 20, and initial disclosures come early
docs.x: Michigan land mine. Interrogatories capped at 20, and initial disclosures come early: Each separately represented party may serve no more than 20 interrogatories on each party, counting discrete subparts. Initial disclosures, including legal theories and expert subject areas, are due without a request: a pleader serves within 14 days after an opposing party answers, and an answering party within the later of 14 days after those are due or 28 days after answering; discovery generally cannot be sought until you serve your own. (MCR 2.309(A)(2); MCR 2.302(A)(1), (A)(5); MCR 2.301(A))

docs.t: Michigan — Setting aside a default needs a verified meritorious defense
docs.x: Michigan land mine. Setting aside a default needs a verified meritorious defense: Except for lack of jurisdiction, a motion to set aside a default or default judgment requires good cause plus a verified statement of facts showing a meritorious defense. If you were personally served, file before the default judgment or within 21 days after it (MCR 2.612 relief aside). Setting aside is conditioned on paying taxable costs. (MCR 2.603(D))

docs.t: Michigan — Pro hac vice: Bar filing first, 5 cases per 365 days
docs.x: Michigan land mine. Pro hac vice: Bar filing first, 5 cases per 365 days: Filing a pro hac vice motion straight with the court will not work. The papers and fee go to the State Bar first, the Bar reports within 7 days, and the court cannot grant the motion until it gets that report. Out-of-state lawyers are limited to five temporary admissions in any 365-day period unless a BLE Rule 5 application is pending. (MCR 8.126(B)(2)–(3), (C)(2)–(3))

docs.t: Michigan — Unpublished Court of Appeals opinions: not binding, and citing them has rules
docs.x: Michigan land mine. Unpublished Court of Appeals opinions: not binding, and citing them has rules: Unpublished opinions are not binding precedent and should not be cited where published authority exists. When citing one, explain why and include the docket number and date (attach a copy if issued before 1996). Published opinions issued on or after November 1, 1990 bind later panels until reversed or overruled through the conflict-panel procedure. (MCR 7.215(C), (J)(1); MCR 2.119(A)(2))

docs.t: Michigan — Protected personal identifying information stays out of public filings
docs.x: Michigan land mine. Protected personal identifying information stays out of public filings: Do not put dates of birth, Social Security numbers, driver’s license or state ID numbers, passport numbers, or financial account numbers in public court filings. Use the redaction and SCAO-form procedure in MCR 1.109(D)(9); where an SSN is required, use only the last four digits. (MCR 1.109(D)(9))

docs.t: Michigan anti-SLAPP — Statute and scope: Uniform Public Expression Protection Act (eff. March 24, 2026)
docs.x: Michigan anti-SLAPP. Statute and scope: Uniform Public Expression Protection Act (eff. March 24, 2026): Michigan now has an anti-SLAPP law. The Uniform Public Expression Protection Act, 2025 PA 52, took effect March 24, 2026, and applies to civil actions filed, or causes of action asserted, on or after that date (Sec. 13). It covers claims based on (i) a communication in a legislative, executive, judicial, administrative, or other governmental proceeding; (ii) a communication on an issue under consideration or review in such a proceeding; or (iii) the exercise of speech, press, assembly, petition, or association rights under the U.S. or Michigan Constitution on a matter of public concern. Excluded: claims against sellers or lessors of goods or services arising from communications about their sale or lease (creative, journalistic, and political works are carved back in), and claims by ind

docs.t: Michigan anti-SLAPP — Procedure: special motion within 60 days; automatic stay
docs.x: Michigan anti-SLAPP. Procedure: special motion within 60 days; automatic stay: File a ‘special motion for expedited relief’ to dismiss all or part of the action no later than 60 days after service of the pleading asserting the claim, or later for good cause. Under MCR 2.114 it must meet MCR 2.119 requirements, say it is a special motion under MCL 691.1853 et seq., and state the basis under MCL 691.1857. Filing stays all other proceedings between the movant and the responding party, including discovery and pending motions. On motion, the court may stay related hearings or discovery involving other parties. The stay lasts until the ruling and the time to appeal expire. The court may allow limited, specific discovery. A fee motion is not stayed, and parties can still voluntarily dismiss or sever. The court must hear the motion within 60 days after filing (or within 60 days after ordering li

docs.t: Michigan anti-SLAPP — Standard: dismissal with prejudice unless the plaintiff makes a prima facie case
docs.x: Michigan anti-SLAPP. Standard: dismissal with prejudice unless the plaintiff makes a prima facie case: The court considers the pleadings, motion papers, affidavits, depositions, admissions, and other documentary evidence. It must dismiss with prejudice if (a) the movant shows the claim is eligible, (b) the responding party fails to show an exclusion applies, and (c) either the responding party fails to establish a prima facie case on each essential element, or the movant shows failure to state a claim or no genuine issue of material fact. (MCL 691.1856, 691.1857(1); MCR 2.114(D)(2)–(3))

docs.t: Michigan anti-SLAPP — Fees: mandatory for a winning movant
docs.x: Michigan anti-SLAPP. Fees: mandatory for a winning movant: The court must award court costs, reasonable attorney fees, and reasonable litigation expenses related to the motion to a prevailing movant. A prevailing respondent gets them only if the motion was frivolous or filed solely to delay. A voluntary dismissal with prejudice counts as the movant prevailing; a dismissal without prejudice does not stop the movant from getting a ruling and fees. (MCL 691.1857(2)–(3), 691.1860; MCR 2.114(F))

docs.t: Michigan anti-SLAPP — Appeal: as of right within 21 days; whole case stayed
docs.x: Michigan anti-SLAPP. Appeal: as of right within 21 days; whole case stayed: The statute gives the moving party an appeal as of right from an order denying the motion in whole or in part, filed within 21 days after entry. MCR 2.114(E) goes further, allowing the movant to appeal as of right from an order ‘denying or granting, in whole or in part’, filed under MCR 7.204. Once any party appeals the ruling, all proceedings between all parties are stayed until the appeal ends (stays on appeal are governed by MCR 7.209 and 7.305(J)). The rule does not give the responding party (plaintiff) an appeal of right from a grant that leaves claims pending; a full dismissal is a final judgment. (MCL 691.1859, 691.1854(3); MCR 2.114(C)(4), (E); MCR 7.204(A)(1))

docs.t: Michigan appeal deadline — Claim of appeal (civil appeal of right)
docs.x: Michigan appellate deadline. Claim of appeal (civil appeal of right): 21 days from Entry of the final judgment or order, or entry of an order deciding a timely postjudgment motion (MCR 7.204(A)(1)). Jurisdictional. File in the Court of Appeals with the entry fee.

docs.t: Michigan appeal deadline — Application for leave to appeal (Court of Appeals)
docs.x: Michigan appellate deadline. Application for leave to appeal (Court of Appeals): 21 days from Entry of the order or judgment, or of an order deciding a timely postjudgment motion (MCR 7.205(A)(1)). Jurisdictional.

docs.t: Michigan appeal deadline — Delayed application for leave (civil)
docs.x: Michigan appellate deadline. Delayed application for leave (civil): 6 months days from Entry of the judgment or order (MCR 7.205(A)(4)(a)). Discretionary; explain the delay.

docs.t: Michigan appeal deadline — Delayed application after dismissal of a timely claim for lack of jurisdiction
docs.x: Michigan appellate deadline. Delayed application after dismissal of a timely claim for lack of jurisdiction: 21 days from Entry of the dismissal order or order denying reconsideration (MCR 7.205(A)(4)(b)).

docs.t: Michigan appeal deadline — Tolling postjudgment motion (new trial, reconsideration, relief)
docs.x: Michigan appellate deadline. Tolling postjudgment motion (new trial, reconsideration, relief): 21 days from Entry of judgment (MCR 7.204(A)(1)(d); MCR 2.611(B); MCR 2.119(F)(1)). Must be filed within the initial 21-day period to toll.

docs.t: Michigan appeal deadline — Late-served judgment: claim of appeal
docs.x: Michigan appellate deadline. Late-served judgment: claim of appeal: 14 days from Service of the judgment (if served late under MCR 2.602) (MCR 7.204(A)(3)). Requires an affidavit showing late service.

docs.t: Michigan appeal deadline — Appellee appearance
docs.x: Michigan appellate deadline. Appellee appearance: 14 days from Service of the claim of appeal (MCR 7.204(G)). Optional, but needed to receive notice.

docs.t: Michigan appeal deadline — Docketing statement
docs.x: Michigan appellate deadline. Docketing statement: 28 days from Filing of the claim of appeal (or cross-appeal, or certification of order granting leave) (MCR 7.204(H); MCR 7.205(E)(3)). Civil appeals only.

docs.t: Michigan appeal deadline — Claim of cross-appeal
docs.x: Michigan appellate deadline. Claim of cross-appeal: 21 days from Later of filing or service of the claim of appeal; or certification of order granting leave (MCR 7.207(B)).

docs.t: Michigan appeal deadline — Answer to application for leave (Court of Appeals)
docs.x: Michigan appellate deadline. Answer to application for leave (Court of Appeals): 21 days from Service of the application (MCR 7.205(C)).

docs.t: Michigan appeal deadline — Appellant’s brief (ordinary civil)
docs.x: Michigan appellate deadline. Appellant’s brief (ordinary civil): 56 days from Latest of claim of appeal, certified leave order, transcript filing, or settled statement (MCR 7.212(A)(1)(a)(iii)). One 28-day extension by stipulation; more by motion. Custody/guardianship: 28 days.

docs.t: Michigan appeal deadline — Appellee’s brief (ordinary civil)
docs.x: Michigan appellate deadline. Appellee’s brief (ordinary civil): 35 days from Service of appellant’s brief (MCR 7.212(A)(2)(a)(ii)). One 28-day extension by stipulation.

docs.t: Michigan appeal deadline — Reply brief
docs.x: Michigan appellate deadline. Reply brief: 21 days from Service of appellee’s brief (MCR 7.212(G)). 3,200 words.

docs.t: Michigan appeal deadline — Motion for reconsideration (Court of Appeals)
docs.x: Michigan appellate deadline. Motion for reconsideration (Court of Appeals): 21 days from Date of the order or date stamped on the opinion (MCR 7.215(I)(1)). 3,200 words; late motions not accepted.

docs.t: Michigan appeal deadline — Request to publish an opinion
docs.x: Michigan appellate deadline. Request to publish an opinion: 21 days from Release of the unpublished opinion (or denial of rehearing) (MCR 7.215(D)(1)).

docs.t: Michigan appeal deadline — Supreme Court application (civil)
docs.x: Michigan appellate deadline. Supreme Court application (civil): 42 days from Court of Appeals decision, order denying timely reconsideration, or grant of publication (MCR 7.305(C)(2)). 56 days in criminal cases.

docs.t: Michigan appeal deadline — Supreme Court application from interlocutory Court of Appeals order
docs.x: Michigan appellate deadline. Supreme Court application from interlocutory Court of Appeals order: 28 days from The Court of Appeals order (MCR 7.305(C)(3)).

docs.t: Michigan appeal deadline — Supreme Court bypass application
docs.x: Michigan appellate deadline. Supreme Court bypass application: 42 days from Filing of claim, application, or original action in the Court of Appeals (MCR 7.305(C)(1)).

docs.t: Michigan appeal deadline — Answer to Supreme Court application
docs.x: Michigan appellate deadline. Answer to Supreme Court application: 28 days from Service of the application (MCR 7.305(D)). Reply within 21 days after service of the answer (MCR 7.305(E)).

docs.t: Michigan appeal deadline — Supreme Court motion for rehearing
docs.x: Michigan appellate deadline. Supreme Court motion for rehearing: 21 days from Filing of the opinion (MCR 7.311(F)(1)). 16,000 words.

docs.t: Michigan appeal deadline — Anti-SLAPP (UPEPA) appeal by moving party
docs.x: Michigan appellate deadline. Anti-SLAPP (UPEPA) appeal by moving party: 21 days from Entry of the order on the special motion (MCL 691.1859; MCR 2.114(E)). Appeal of right; all proceedings stayed.

docs.t: Michigan appeal deadline — Appeal of right to circuit court (from district/probate court or agency)
docs.x: Michigan appellate deadline. Appeal of right to circuit court (from district/probate court or agency): 21 days from Entry of the judgment, order, or decision, or order deciding a timely postjudgment motion (MCR 7.104(A)). Jurisdictional; unless a statute sets another time.

docs.t: Minnesota — Hip-pocket service: the action starts at service, and you must file within one year or lose it with prejudice
docs.x: Minnesota land mine. Hip-pocket service: the action starts at service, and you must file within one year or lose it with prejudice: A Minnesota civil action is commenced by service of the summons (or a signed waiver, or delivery to the sheriff followed by service within 60 days), not by filing. A case that is not filed with the court within one year after commencement against any party is deemed dismissed with prejudice against all parties, unless all parties signed a stipulation within that year to extend. Family cases are excepted. Calendar the one-year date the day you serve. (Minn. R. Civ. P. 3.01, 5.04(a))

docs.t: Minnesota — Do not plead a dollar figure over $50,000
docs.x: Minnesota land mine. Do not plead a dollar figure over $50,000: If unliquidated damages over $50,000 are sought, the complaint must state only that reasonable damages greater than $50,000 are sought. Amounts under $50,000 must be stated. (Minn. R. Civ. P. 8.01)

docs.t: Minnesota — Appeals from orders run from service of notice of filing, not entry
docs.x: Minnesota land mine. Appeals from orders run from service of notice of filing, not entry: Appeal a judgment within 60 days after its entry. Appeal an appealable order within 60 days after any party serves written notice of its filing; the court administrator’s own notice does not start the clock (Minn. R. Civ. P. 77.04). If you won, serve notice of filing to start the appeal period. Once the time to appeal the judgment expires, earlier orders can no longer be appealed (Rule 104.02). (Minn. R. Civ. App. P. 104.01, subd. 1; 104.02; Minn. R. Civ. P. 77.04)

docs.t: Minnesota — A Rule 60 motion tolls the appeal time only if filed within new-trial time, and a premature notice of appeal is void
docs.x: Minnesota land mine. A Rule 60 motion tolls the appeal time only if filed within new-trial time, and a premature notice of appeal is void: Timely motions under Rules 50.02, 52.02, 59, and (if filed within the new-trial deadline) 60 restart the appeal period from service of notice of filing of the order deciding the last motion. A notice of appeal filed while such a motion is pending is ‘premature and of no effect’; you must file a new one. A new-trial motion must be served within 30 days after a general verdict or service of notice of filing of the decision, and heard within 60 days. (Minn. R. Civ. App. P. 104.01, subds. 2–3; Minn. R. Civ. P. 59.03)

docs.t: Minnesota — Use the notice to remove early or lose it
docs.x: Minnesota land mine. Use the notice to remove early or lose it: The peremptory notice to remove must be served and filed within 10 days after notice of the assigned judge. It cannot be used against a judge who has already ruled on a motion or presided at another proceeding you had notice of. (Minn. R. Civ. P. 63.03)

docs.t: Minnesota — Anti-SLAPP: 60 days to move, 30 days to appeal
docs.x: Minnesota land mine. Anti-SLAPP: 60 days to move, 30 days to appeal: The UPEPA motion is due within 60 days after service of the pleading (later only for good cause), and an appeal from denial must be filed within 30 days after entry of the order, not the general 60 days. Fees to a prevailing movant are mandatory, and a plaintiff’s voluntary dismissal does not avoid them. (Minn. Stat. §§ 554.09, 554.13(b)–(c), 554.15, 554.16)

docs.t: Minnesota — No discovery until the Rule 26.06 conference and plan
docs.x: Minnesota land mine. No discovery until the Rule 26.06 conference and plan: Parties may not seek discovery from any source before conferring and preparing a discovery plan, except in exempt proceedings or by stipulation or order. The conference must happen within 30 days from the initial answer due date, and the written plan must be filed within 14 days after the conference. Early Rule 34 requests may be delivered 21 days after service but are deemed served at the conference. Initial disclosures are due within 60 days after the original answer due date. (Minn. R. Civ. P. 26.01(a)(3), 26.04(a)–(b), 26.06(a)–(b))

docs.t: Minnesota — Dispositive motions: 28 days’ notice, and summary judgment cutoff
docs.x: Minnesota land mine. Dispositive motions: 28 days’ notice, and summary judgment cutoff: Dispositive motion papers (notice, motion, proposed order, affidavits, memorandum) must be served and filed at least 28 days before the hearing, or the hearing may be canceled. docs.x: Minnesota land mine. docs.x: Minnesota land mine. Prac. 115.11; Minn. R. Civ. App. P. 104.01, subd. 2)

docs.t: Minnesota anti-SLAPP — Scope and the long list of exclusions
docs.x: Minnesota anti-SLAPP. Scope and the long list of exclusions: Covers a cause of action based on the defendant’s (1) communication in a governmental proceeding, (2) communication on an issue under review in a governmental proceeding, or (3) exercise of speech, press, assembly, petition, or association rights under the U.S. or Minnesota Constitution on a matter of public concern. Minnesota added exclusions beyond the uniform act: claims against government units; certain public-health enforcement; commercial speech by sellers about their goods or services; crime-victim suits; real-property possession and title suits; bodily injury and wrongful death (unless reputation damage is claimed); insurance-code and insurance-contract claims; common-law fraud; family-law chapters 517–519A and protection, harassment, and vulnerable-adult orders; employment claims under chapters 175, 177, 178, 179, 179A

docs.x: Minnesota anti-SLAPP. Procedure: 60 days to move, automatic stay, 60-day hearing and ruling clocks: File the special motion for expedited relief within 60 days after being served with the pleading that asserts the claim, or later for good cause (§ 554.09). Filing stays all other proceedings between the movant and the responding party, including discovery, until the ruling and the time to appeal it run out; the court may stay matters involving other parties on motion. Fee motions, voluntary dismissals, severance, unrelated motions, and public-safety injunctions are not stayed. The court must hear the motion within 60 days after filing (extendable for allowed discovery or good cause) and rule within 60 days after the hearing (§§ 554.11, 554.14). docs.t: Minnesota anti-SLAPP — Fees are mandatory for a prevailing movant
docs.x: Minnesota anti-SLAPP. Fees are mandatory for a prevailing movant: The court shall award court costs, reasonable attorney fees, and reasonable litigation expenses related to the motion to a prevailing movant. A prevailing responding party gets fees only if the motion was frivolous or filed solely to delay. A plaintiff cannot dodge fees by dismissing: a voluntary dismissal without prejudice does not defeat the movant’s right to a ruling and fees, and a dismissal with prejudice counts as the movant prevailing (§ 554.13(b)–(c)). (Minn. Stat. §§ 554.13(b)–(c), 554.16)

docs.t: Minnesota anti-SLAPP — Appeal: 30 days, as of right, and the whole case stops
docs.x: Minnesota anti-SLAPP. Appeal: 30 days, as of right, and the whole case stops: A moving party may appeal as of right from an order denying the motion in whole or in part. The appeal must be filed within 30 days after entry of the order, half the usual 60-day civil appeal period under Minn. R. Civ. App. P. 104.01. While the appeal is pending, all proceedings between all parties are stayed (§ 554.10(c)). The statute grants the special appeal of right only to the moving party; a responding party whose claim is dismissed must use the ordinary appeal rules. The act must be broadly construed to protect speech, press, assembly, petition, and association rights (§ 554.17) and construed for uniformity with other enacting states (§ 554.18). (Minn. Stat. §§ 554.10(c), 554.15, 554.17, 554.18; Minn. R. Civ. App. P. 104.01)

docs.x: Minnesota appellate deadline. Notice of appeal from a judgment: 60 days from Entry of the judgment (Minn. R. Civ. App. P. 104.01, subd. 1). Unless a statute sets a different time. Not extendable by the appellate court (Rule 126.02).

docs.t: Minnesota appeal deadline — Motion for new trial (service)
docs.x: Minnesota appellate deadline. Motion for new trial (service): 30 days from General verdict, or service of notice of filing of the decision or order (Minn. R. Civ. P. 59.03). Must be heard within 60 days. JMOL (50.02) and amended findings (52.02) use the same times.

docs.t: Minnesota appeal deadline — Petition for discretionary review (Court of Appeals)
docs.x: Minnesota appellate deadline. Petition for discretionary review (Court of Appeals): 30 days from Filing of the order (Minn. R. Civ. App. P. 105.01). Response 7 days; reply 3 days. Also the deadline for class-certification appeals (Minn. R. Civ. P. 23.06).

docs.x: Minnesota appellate deadline. Order transcript / file notice re record: 14 days from Filing the notice of appeal (Minn. R. Civ. App. P. 110.02, subd. 1). Transcript certificate due 14 days after ordering.

docs.t: Minnesota appeal deadline — Petition for review (Supreme Court)

docs.x: Minnesota appellate deadline. Petition for rehearing (Supreme Court only): 14 days from Filing of the Supreme Court decision or order (Minn. R. Civ. App. P. 140.01). None in the Court of Appeals. $100 fee.

docs.x: Minnesota appellate deadline. Recusal motion, Court of Appeals: 7 days from Notice of oral argument or nonoral conference (or panel change) (Minn. R. Civ. App. P. 141.02(b)). Supreme Court: 14 days after the case-initiating filing or grant of review (Rule 141.01(b)).

docs.t: Missouri — Tort venue is where the plaintiff was first injured
docs.x: Missouri land mine. Tort venue is where the plaintiff was first injured: If any count sounds in tort and the injury occurred in Missouri, venue lies only in the county of first injury (for defamation or privacy, where first published; for exposure, where it happened, not where symptoms appeared). Joinder cannot create venue, adding or dropping parties can force a transfer, an improper-venue motion is deemed granted if not denied within 90 days, and an erroneous denial requires reversal. (RSMo 508.010.4, .8–.10, .14, .16; 507.040; 508.012)

docs.x: Missouri land mine. Punitive damages cannot be pleaded at the start: An initial petition may not claim punitive damages. You need leave on a supported motion filed at least 120 days before the final pretrial conference or trial. (RSMo 510.261.5)

docs.t: Missouri — Medical-negligence affidavit within 90 days
docs.x: Missouri land mine. Medical-negligence affidavit within 90 days: In any health care negligence case, file a separate affidavit for each defendant within 90 days after filing the petition (extendable once for up to 90 days for good cause), stating that you have a qualifying provider’s written opinion. docs.x: Missouri land mine. Two-year limits for defamation, assault, and medical malpractice: Libel, slander, injurious falsehood, assault, battery, false imprisonment, and malicious prosecution must be sued within 2 years, and medical malpractice within 2 years of the act of neglect (with narrow exceptions). Most other torts and contracts have 5 years, and written promises to pay money have 10. (RSMo 516.140, 516.105, 516.120, 516.110)

docs.x: Missouri land mine. Notice of appeal: 10 days after the judgment becomes final: No appeal is effective unless the notice of appeal is filed within 10 days after the judgment or order becomes final. When a judgment becomes final is set by Supreme Court Rule (Rules 81–84, not collected), so compute the date from the rule, not from the date of entry. A late appeal requires a special order of the appellate court. (RSMo 512.050, 512.060)

docs.x: Missouri land mine. docs.x: Missouri land mine. docs.x: Missouri land mine. Fee-sharing with non-lawyers is a crime: Dividing fees with a non-lawyer, or a firm not wholly made up of licensed attorneys, is a misdemeanor with treble-damages exposure. This is stricter than an ethics-rule violation alone. (RSMo 484.150)

docs.t: Missouri anti-SLAPP — New Uniform Public Expression Protection Act, effective August 28, 2026
docs.x: Missouri anti-SLAPP. New Uniform Public Expression Protection Act, effective August 28, 2026: Missouri repealed its narrow anti-SLAPP statute (§ 537.528) and enacted the Uniform Public Expression Protection Act, § 537.529 (S.B. 835 & 1111 merged with S.B. 1067, 2026). It covers claims based on communications in a legislative, executive, judicial, administrative, or other governmental proceeding, communications on an issue under consideration in such a proceeding, or exercise of speech, press, assembly, petition, or association rights under the U.S. or Missouri Constitution on a matter of public concern. It must be broadly construed. It applies to civil actions filed, and causes of action asserted, on or after August 28, 2026. The collected text does not say whether old § 537.528 still governs claims filed earlier. (RSMo 537.529.1, .3, .13, .15; RSMo 537.528 (repealed eff. Aug. 28, 2026))

docs.t: Missouri anti-SLAPP — Exemptions: government defendants, enforcement actions, and commercial speech
docs.x: Missouri anti-SLAPP. Exemptions: government defendants, enforcement actions, and commercial speech: The Act does not apply to claims against a governmental unit or its employee acting officially; to claims by a governmental unit enforcing a law against an imminent threat to public health or safety; or to claims against a business arising from communications about its sale or lease of goods or services. Dramatic, literary, musical, political, journalistic, and artistic works are not “goods or services.” (RSMo 537.529.4)

docs.t: Missouri anti-SLAPP — Procedure: file within 60 days of service; automatic stay
docs.x: Missouri anti-SLAPP. Procedure: file within 60 days of service; automatic stay: File a special motion to dismiss within 60 days after being served with the pleading asserting the claim (later for good cause). Filing stays all other proceedings between movant and respondent, including discovery and pending motions, until the ruling and the time to appeal expire. The court may also stay related hearings or discovery involving other parties. Limited discovery is allowed only if specific information is needed and not otherwise available. The court must hear the motion within 60 days after filing (later for allowed discovery or good cause) and rule within 60 days after the hearing. A fee motion, voluntary dismissal, and severance are not stayed. (RSMo 537.529.5–.7, .10)

docs.t: Missouri anti-SLAPP — Standard: three-step test with summary-judgment evidence
docs.x: Missouri anti-SLAPP. Standard: three-step test with summary-judgment evidence: The court dismisses with prejudice if (1) the movant shows the Act applies, (2) the respondent fails to show an exemption, and (3) either the respondent fails to establish a prima facie case on each essential element, or the movant shows failure to state a claim or no genuine issue of material fact. The court considers pleadings, the motion and responses, and any evidence admissible on summary judgment. A voluntary dismissal without prejudice does not defeat the motion; one with prejudice makes the movant the prevailing party. (RSMo 537.529.8–.9)

docs.t: Missouri anti-SLAPP — Fees: mandatory for a winning movant
docs.x: Missouri anti-SLAPP. Fees: mandatory for a winning movant: The court must award costs, reasonable attorney’s fees, and reasonable litigation expenses related to the motion to a prevailing movant. A prevailing respondent recovers them only if the motion was frivolous or filed solely to delay. (RSMo 537.529.12)

docs.t: Missouri anti-SLAPP — Appeal: 21 days, as of right, from a denial
docs.x: Missouri anti-SLAPP. Appeal: 21 days, as of right, from a denial: A moving party may appeal as of right within 21 days from an order denying the motion in whole or in part. Once any party appeals a ruling on the motion, all proceedings between all parties are stayed until the appeal ends. (RSMo 537.529.11, .6(3))

docs.t: Missouri anti-SLAPP — Old § 537.528 (pre-August 28, 2026 cases)
docs.x: Missouri anti-SLAPP. Old § 537.528 (pre-August 28, 2026 cases): The repealed statute applied only to actions over conduct or speech in connection with a public hearing or public meeting in a quasi-judicial proceeding before a state or local body. It required priority consideration of a special motion to dismiss, judgment on the pleadings, or summary judgment; suspended discovery; mandated fees if such a motion filed within 90 days of the answer was granted; and allowed an expedited appeal. (RSMo 537.528 (2012 version, repealed by L. 2026 S.B. 835 & 1111 merged with S.B. 1067))

docs.t: Missouri appeal deadline — Notice of appeal
docs.x: Missouri appellate deadline. Notice of appeal: 10 days from Judgment or order appealed from becomes final (RSMo 512.050). Finality timing is set by Supreme Court Rule (Rules 81–84), not collected; verify.

docs.x: Missouri appellate deadline. Late notice of appeal by special order of appellate court: 180 days from Date of final judgment (RSMo 512.060). The statute says six months; the current Supreme Court Rule may differ; not verified.

docs.t: Missouri appeal deadline — Appeal from denial of UPEPA (anti-SLAPP) special motion to dismiss
docs.x: Missouri appellate deadline. Appeal from denial of UPEPA (anti-SLAPP) special motion to dismiss: 21 days from Order denying the motion in whole or in part (RSMo 537.529.11). Actions filed on or after Aug. 28, 2026.

docs.t: Missouri appeal deadline — Transcript filed and case transferred to appellate court
docs.x: Missouri appellate deadline. Transcript filed and case transferred to appellate court: 90 days from Filing of notice of appeal (RSMo 512.130). Trial court may extend under RSMo 506.060.2.

docs.x: Missouri appellate deadline. Pay court reporter for transcript: 10 days from Ordering the transcript (or the reporter’s written estimate) (RSMo 512.050).

docs.t: Missouri appeal deadline — File supersedeas bond after court sets amount
docs.x: Missouri appellate deadline. File supersedeas bond after court sets amount: 20 days from Order fixing bond (maximum allowed) (RSMo 512.080.1(2)). Bond must be presented at or before filing the notice of appeal unless time is allowed.

docs.t: Missouri appeal deadline — New-trial motion deemed denied
docs.x: Missouri appellate deadline. New-trial motion deemed denied: 90 days from Filing of the motion (RSMo 510.360). Statutory; confirm against the current Supreme Court Rule.

docs.t: Missouri appeal deadline — Court’s own order of new trial; setting aside judgment for good cause
docs.x: Missouri appellate deadline. Court’s own order of new trial; setting aside judgment for good cause: 30 days from Entry of judgment (RSMo 510.370, 511.060). Statutory; confirm against the current Supreme Court Rule.

docs.t: Missouri appeal deadline — Application for trial de novo (associate circuit cases under ch. 482, 535, municipal)
docs.x: Missouri appellate deadline. Application for trial de novo (associate circuit cases under ch. 482, 535, municipal): 10 days from Judgment rendered (RSMo 512.190).

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands — Post-trial motions: 10 days, not 28
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands land mine. Post-trial motions: 10 days, not 28: A Rule 59(e) motion to alter or amend is due 10 days after entry of judgment. So are a Rule 50(b) renewed motion for judgment as a matter of law and a Rule 52(b) motion to amend findings. A motion for a new trial is due in 20 days, and the court’s own power to order a new trial ends at 20 days. The federal rule allows 28 days for each. The court cannot extend any of these deadlines. Because 10 days is “10 days or less,” intermediate weekends and holidays are skipped, but do not rely on that cushion. (NMI R. Civ. P. 50(b), 52(b), 59(b), (d), (e), 6(a)(1)(D), 6(b)(2))

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands — A late post-judgment motion does not toll the appeal
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands land mine. A late post-judgment motion does not toll the appeal: The 30-day appeal clock restarts only for motions filed “within the time allotted” by the NMI civil rules. A Rule 59(e) motion filed on day 20 under the federal habit is untimely and does not toll. A Rule 60 motion tolls only if filed within 28 days after judgment. The Supreme Court cannot extend the notice-of-appeal deadline except under Rule 4(a)(5)–(6). (NMI Sup. Ct. R. 4(a)(1), 4(a)(4)(A), 26(b)(1))

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands — 30 days to appeal, even when the government is a party
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands land mine. 30 days to appeal, even when the government is a party: File the notice of appeal with the Superior Court clerk, not the Supreme Court, within 30 days after entry. There is no 60-day period for government cases as in federal court. Other parties get 14 days after the first notice, or the regular 30 days if that ends later. Pay the $175 fee when you file. (NMI Sup. Ct. R. 3(a)(1), 3(e), 4(a)(1), 4(a)(3); Fee Schedule item 81)

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands — No separate judgment document means a 150-day wait
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands land mine. No separate judgment document means a 150-day wait: The notice of appeal must attach the judgment or order being appealed. In a civil case that means a separate entry of judgment. Without a separate document, the judgment is treated as entered only after 150 days have run from its docketing. A premature notice is held until the separate judgment is filed. (NMI Sup. Ct. R. 3(c)(1)(B) & note 1, 4(a)(2), 4(a)(7)(A)(ii))

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands — Pro hac vice is $5,000 and one new case a year
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands land mine. Pro hac vice is $5,000 and one new case a year: The fee is $5,000 per application, and you may apply in only one new case per calendar year. You cannot seek admission in a second case until the first is closed. Admission lapses after 12 months, and renewing requires a new application and a new fee. Budget for it, and plan for long cases. (NMI Sup. Ct. R. 73-1(c), (f); Fee Schedule item 116)

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands — Off-island counsel need active local counsel
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands land mine. Off-island counsel need active local counsel: Even a CNMI-admitted lawyer without a regular Commonwealth office must associate local counsel. Local counsel must take a meaningful part in preparing and trying the case and attend proceedings. Service on local counsel binds you. (NMI R. Civ. P. 5(b)(4))

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands — Motions must be filed 30 days before the hearing; opposition is due in 9
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands land mine. Motions must be filed 30 days before the hearing; opposition is due in 9: Do not choose a hearing date yourself; the clerk sets it. Your opposition is due 9 days after the motion is served, which is 9 days excluding weekends and holidays. It is not keyed to the hearing date as in many state courts. A memorandum over 25 pages filed without permission may be struck. (NMI R. Civ. P. 6(c)(1)–(2), 7(b)(5)–(6))

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands — Jury demand: 60 days, a $400 fee, and 6 unanimous jurors
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands land mine. Jury demand: 60 days, a $400 fee, and 6 unanimous jurors: Serve the jury demand no later than 60 days after the last pleading is filed. Pay the non-refundable $400 jury fee on or before the day the demand is filed; without proper service, filing, and payment, the jury is waived. A proper demand can be withdrawn only by consent and no later than 45 days before trial. The verdict must be unanimous and returned by 6 jurors. Jury trials also require advance deposits: $1,500 for trials of less than 5 business days, plus $500 for each added day. (NMI R. Civ. P. 38(b), (d), (f), 48(b); Fee Schedule items 48–49)

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands — No mail service in the last 10 days before a hearing or trial
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands land mine. No mail service in the last 10 days before a hearing or trial: Papers about a motion with a set hearing date, or about a matter set for trial, may not be served by mail within 10 days of the hearing or trial date. Use e-service or hand delivery. (NMI R. Civ. P. 5(b)(2)(C))

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands — Supreme Court docketing statement within 15 days or risk dismissal
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands land mine. Supreme Court docketing statement within 15 days or risk dismissal: Within 15 days after the Clerk gives notice that the appeal is docketed, file the docketing statement (Form 2). Extensions are disfavored, and failing to file is grounds for dismissal. Also within 15 days after filing the notice of appeal, order transcripts on Form 3 or certify that none will be ordered. Opposing counsel must respond or file an appearance within 10 days after being served with the docketing statement. (NMI Sup. Ct. R. 3-1(a)(4)–(5), 3-1(b), 11-1(b)(1))

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands — Briefs: 35 pages including everything
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands land mine. Briefs: 35 pages including everything: A principal brief is limited to 35 pages and a reply to 20, “inclusive of the caption, headings, table of contents, etc.” The limit is pages, not words. Briefs use 11-point Times New Roman with 1.5 spacing. A brief that does not conform may be struck, fined, or lead to dismissal. Only one automatic 30-day extension is available per brief. (NMI Sup. Ct. R. 31-1(a)(1), 32(a)(4)–(7), 32(i))

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands — Slander has a 2-year limit
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands land mine. Slander has a 2-year limit: Actions for slander, assault and battery, false imprisonment, medical malpractice, and wrongful death or personal injury must be filed within 2 years. Most other actions get 6 years. Do not assume a one-year defamation period as in many states, or a three-year one. (7 CMC §§ 2503, 2505)

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands anti-SLAPP — No anti-SLAPP statute found in the Commonwealth Code
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands anti-SLAPP. No anti-SLAPP statute found in the Commonwealth Code: The CNMI has no anti-SLAPP statute that could be found. Searches of the Law Revision Commission’s official Commonwealth Code (by section title, for “SLAPP,” “strategic lawsuit,” “public participation,” and “special motion”) and its site-wide search across public laws, the Code, and the Commonwealth Register found no anti-SLAPP law. The only site-wide “SLAPP” hit was the word “slapping” in a 2025 child-care regulation. Title 7 (Civil Procedure) has no chapter on the subject. There is no special motion to strike, discovery stay, or fee-shifting rule tied to speech or petitioning in the collected civil or appellate rules. Related speech-tort rules that do exist: the Uniform Single Publication Act (one cause of action per publication, 7 CMC § 2411), and a 2-year limitation for slander (7 CMC § 2503(a))

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands appeal deadline — Notice of appeal (civil)
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands appellate deadline. Notice of appeal (civil): 30 days from Entry of the judgment or order (separate document, or 150 days after docketing) (NMI Sup. Ct. R. 4(a)(1), 4(a)(7)). File with the Superior Court clerk. No 60-day period for government cases. Restarts after timely tolling motions.

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands appeal deadline — Notice of appeal by another party (cross-appeal)
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands appellate deadline. Notice of appeal by another party (cross-appeal): 14 days from Filing of the first notice of appeal (NMI Sup. Ct. R. 4(a)(3)). Or within the regular 30 days if that ends later.

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands appeal deadline — Motion to extend time to appeal
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands appellate deadline. Motion to extend time to appeal: 30 days from Expiration of the original appeal deadline (NMI Sup. Ct. R. 4(a)(5)). Filed in the Superior Court; requires excusable neglect or good cause. The extension cannot exceed 30 days past the original deadline or 14 days after the order granting it, whichever is later.

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands appeal deadline — Motion to reopen time to appeal
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands appellate deadline. Motion to reopen time to appeal: 180 days from Entry of the judgment or order (NMI Sup. Ct. R. 4(a)(6)). Or 14 days after receiving notice of entry, whichever is earlier. Available only if Rule 77(d) notice was not received within 21 days. Reopens for 14 days.

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands appeal deadline — Renewed JMOL (tolls appeal)
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands appellate deadline. Renewed JMOL (tolls appeal): 10 days from Entry of judgment (or jury discharge if issue undecided) (NMI R. Civ. P. 50(b); NMI Sup. Ct. R. 4(a)(4)(A)(i)). Federal rule allows 28 days. Cannot be extended. Weekends excluded (10 days or less).

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands appeal deadline — Motion to amend findings (tolls appeal)
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands appellate deadline. Motion to amend findings (tolls appeal): 10 days from Entry of judgment (NMI R. Civ. P. 52(b); NMI Sup. Ct. R. 4(a)(4)(A)(ii)). Federal rule allows 28 days. Cannot be extended.

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands appeal deadline — Motion to alter or amend judgment (tolls appeal)
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands appellate deadline. Motion to alter or amend judgment (tolls appeal): 10 days from Entry of judgment (NMI R. Civ. P. 59(e); NMI Sup. Ct. R. 4(a)(4)(A)(iv)). Federal rule allows 28 days. Cannot be extended. Limited to intervening change in law, new evidence, or clear error or manifest injustice.

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands appeal deadline — Motion for new trial (tolls appeal)
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands appellate deadline. Motion for new trial (tolls appeal): 20 days from Entry of judgment (NMI R. Civ. P. 59(b); NMI Sup. Ct. R. 4(a)(4)(A)(v)). Federal rule allows 28 days. Opposing affidavits are due 14 days after service. Cannot be extended.

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands appeal deadline — Attorney-fee motion in Superior Court (tolls appeal)
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands appellate deadline. Attorney-fee motion in Superior Court (tolls appeal): 14 days from Entry of judgment (NMI R. Civ. P. 54(d)(2)(B)(i); NMI Sup. Ct. R. 4(a)(4)(A)(iii)). Unless a statute or court order provides otherwise.

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands appeal deadline — Rule 60 motion that tolls the appeal
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands appellate deadline. Rule 60 motion that tolls the appeal: 28 days from Entry of judgment (NMI Sup. Ct. R. 4(a)(4)(A)(vi)). A Rule 60(b) motion may be filed later (up to 1 year for reasons 1–3), but then it does not toll.

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands appeal deadline — Docketing statement (Form 2)
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands appellate deadline. Docketing statement (Form 2): 15 days from Clerk’s notice that the appeal is docketed (NMI Sup. Ct. R. 3-1(a)(4)). Extensions disfavored; failure is grounds for dismissal. Not required of pro se appellants.

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands appeal deadline — Response to docketing statement or notice of appearance
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands appellate deadline. Response to docketing statement or notice of appearance: 10 days from Service of the docketing statement (NMI Sup. Ct. R. 3-1(b)). File the conflicts notice at the same time (Rule 3-1(c)). Counted excluding weekends (10 days or less).

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands appeal deadline — Representation statement
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands appellate deadline. Representation statement: 15 days from Filing of the notice of appeal (NMI Sup. Ct. R. 12(b)). May be included in the docketing statement.

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands appeal deadline — Transcript order or no-transcript certification (Form 3)
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands appellate deadline. Transcript order or no-transcript certification (Form 3): 15 days from Notice of appeal, or order deciding last tolling motion, if later (NMI Sup. Ct. R. 11-1(b)(1)). Appellee may add portions within 10 days; appellant may respond within 5 days.

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands appeal deadline — Certified transcript designation (Form 4)
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands appellate deadline. Certified transcript designation (Form 4): 15 days from Service of the Rule 11-1(b)(4) completion notice (NMI Sup. Ct. R. 11-1(c)(1), 11-1(d)(1)). Joint or separate. Certified transcript is due within 30 days after Form 4 unless more time is granted.

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands appeal deadline — Appellant’s opening brief and appendix
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands appellate deadline. Appellant’s opening brief and appendix: 40 days from Filing of the certificate of record (NMI Sup. Ct. R. 30(a)(3), 31(a)(1)). 35-page limit, inclusive of everything. One automatic extension of up to 30 days is available.

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands appeal deadline — Appellee’s brief
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands appellate deadline. Appellee’s brief: 30 days from Service of the appellant’s brief (NMI Sup. Ct. R. 31(a)(1)). 35-page limit.

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands appeal deadline — Reply brief
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands appellate deadline. Reply brief: 14 days from Service of the appellee’s brief (NMI Sup. Ct. R. 31(a)(1)). Must be filed at least 3 days before argument. 20-page limit.

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands appeal deadline — Amicus brief
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands appellate deadline. Amicus brief: 7 days from Filing of the supported party’s principal brief (NMI Sup. Ct. R. 29(e)). Half the principal-brief length. Leave or consent needed, except for the Commonwealth.

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands appeal deadline — Response to a motion
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands appellate deadline. Response to a motion: 8 days from Service of the motion (NMI Sup. Ct. R. 27(a)(4)(A)). Reply is due within 5 days after the response. Both are counted excluding weekends and holidays.

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands appeal deadline — Motion to reconsider an order on a motion
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands appellate deadline. Motion to reconsider an order on a motion: 10 days from Service of the order (NMI Sup. Ct. R. 27-2(d)(1)). Response is due within 7 days for orders by the Clerk or a single justice.

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands appeal deadline — Petition for permission to appeal class-certification order
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands appellate deadline. Petition for permission to appeal class-certification order: 14 days from Entry of the order (NMI R. Civ. P. 23(f)). Filed with the Supreme Court clerk; does not stay proceedings unless ordered.

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands appeal deadline — Petition for rehearing
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands appellate deadline. Petition for rehearing: 14 days from Entry of judgment (NMI Sup. Ct. R. 40(a)(1)). 15 pages; no answer unless requested; $250 fee.

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands appeal deadline — Bill of costs
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands appellate deadline. Bill of costs: 14 days from Entry of judgment (NMI Sup. Ct. R. 39(d)(1)). Objections are due within 10 days after service.

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands appeal deadline — Request for appellate attorney fees
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands appellate deadline. Request for appellate attorney fees: 5 days from Expiration of the rehearing period (or disposition of a timely rehearing petition) (NMI Sup. Ct. R. 39-1(a)(1)). Calendar days. File separately from the bill of costs. Opposition due in 10 days; reply in 5.

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands appeal deadline — Issuance of mandate
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands appellate deadline. Issuance of mandate: 7 days from Expiration of rehearing period, or denial of rehearing, stay motion, or fee petition (whichever is later) (NMI Sup. Ct. R. 41(b)). Calendar days. A timely rehearing petition, stay motion, or fee petition stays the mandate.

docs.t: Northern Mariana Islands appeal deadline — Stay of mandate pending U.S. Supreme Court certiorari
docs.x: Northern Mariana Islands appellate deadline. Stay of mandate pending U.S. Supreme Court certiorari: 90 days from Grant of the stay (NMI Sup. Ct. R. 41(d)(2)(B)). Continues until final disposition if the petition is filed and the Clerk notified within the stay period.

docs.t: Mississippi — Post-trial motions: 10 days from entry, and no extensions
docs.x: Mississippi land mine. Post-trial motions: 10 days from entry, and no extensions: Motions for JNOV, amended findings, a new trial, or to alter or amend the judgment are due 10 days after entry of judgment, not 28 as in federal court. The trial court cannot extend them. A Rule 60 motion tolls the appeal time only if it is filed within 10 days after entry of judgment. (M.R.C.P. 6(b), 50(b), 52(b), 59(b), (e); M.R.A.P. 4(d))

docs.t: Mississippi — No appellate extension of the civil appeal deadline
docs.x: Mississippi land mine. No appellate extension of the civil appeal deadline: The notice of appeal is due 30 days after entry of the judgment and is filed with the trial-court clerk. A late notice means mandatory dismissal. Neither appellate court can extend the time to appeal, or to petition for interlocutory appeal, in a civil case. Only the trial court can extend it under Rule 4(g): good cause if you move before the time runs out, excusable neglect if you move within the next 30 days, and the extension can last at most 30 days or 10 days after the order, whichever is later. (M.R.A.P. 2(a)(1), 2(c), 4(a), 4(g), 26(b))

docs.t: Mississippi — Seven days after the notice of appeal: designate the record and deposit costs
docs.x: Mississippi land mine. Seven days after the notice of appeal: designate the record and deposit costs: Within 7 days after filing the notice of appeal, you must: • file and serve a designation of the record; • deposit the estimated record cost with the trial-court clerk; and • file and serve a certificate of compliance. If the court reporter gives no estimate, the deposit is $300 per day of proceedings. Missing these steps does not void the appeal but can lead to sanctions or dismissal. After a deficiency notice, you have 14 days to cure. (M.R.A.P. 2(a)(2), 10(b)(1), 11(b)(1))

docs.t: Mississippi — Answer extensions by agreement: once only, 10 days, filed stipulation
docs.x: Mississippi land mine. Answer extensions by agreement: once only, 10 days, filed stipulation: The answer is due 30 days after service. The parties may extend it only once, by no more than 10 days, and only by a written stipulation of counsel filed in the record. Open-ended courtesy extensions are not authorized by the rule. (M.R.C.P. 12(a))

docs.t: Mississippi — Circuit and county court: discovery closes 90 days after the answer
docs.x: Mississippi land mine. Circuit and county court: discovery closes 90 days after the answer: Unless the court grants leave on a written motion showing good cause, discovery must be completed within 90 days after the defendant serves its answer. Absent special circumstances, an expert not designated at least 60 days before trial may not testify. Discovery responses must restate each request before the answer. A motion to compel must include a good-faith conference certificate and quote each disputed request verbatim. (UCRCCC 4.03)

docs.t: Mississippi — Motion practice: memoranda go to the judge, not the clerk, and unheard motions are abandoned
docs.x: Mississippi land mine. Motion practice: memoranda go to the judge, not the clerk, and unheard motions are abandoned: In circuit court, file the motion with the clerk and mail a copy to the judge. Memoranda on dismissal and summary-judgment motions are mailed to the judge and not filed with the clerk. The response is due within 10 days and the rebuttal within 5. Memoranda are limited to 25 pages. You must attach copies of any authority that is not a Mississippi or federal statute or rule, a U.S. Supreme Court case, or a case in the Southern or Federal Reporter. The movant must bring its motion to hearing: a pretrial motion not pursued before trial is deemed abandoned, and dispositive motions are abandoned unless heard at least 10 days before trial. (UCRCCC 2.04, 4.02)

docs.t: Mississippi — Requests for admission are conclusively admitted after 30 days
docs.x: Mississippi land mine. Requests for admission are conclusively admitted after 30 days: A request for admission is admitted unless a written answer or objection is served within 30 days. A defendant need not answer before 45 days after service of the summons. Deemed admissions are conclusively established unless the court allows withdrawal. (M.R.C.P. 36)

docs.t: Mississippi — Serve within 120 days, and know Mississippi’s mail and residence-service rules
docs.x: Mississippi land mine. Serve within 120 days, and know Mississippi’s mail and residence-service rules: An unserved defendant is dismissed without prejudice after 120 days unless you show good cause. Service by first-class mail works only if the defendant returns the acknowledgment form. Certified mail (return receipt requested) is an added option only for persons outside Mississippi. Residence service is allowed only if personal service cannot be made with reasonable diligence. It requires leaving the papers with the spouse or a family member above 16 and then mailing a copy, and service is complete on the 10th day after mailing. (M.R.C.P. 4(c)(3), 4(c)(5), 4(d)(1)(B), 4(h))

docs.t: Mississippi — Recusal: 30-day deadline from notice of the assigned judge
docs.x: Mississippi land mine. Recusal: 30-day deadline from notice of the assigned judge: A recusal motion must be supported by an affidavit and filed within 30 days after the parties are told which judge is assigned. The only exception is facts that could not reasonably have been known then. Review of a denial is by petition to the Supreme Court within 14 days. (UCRCCC 1.15; UCCR 1.11; M.R.A.P. 48B)

docs.t: Mississippi — Pro hac vice: local counsel must attend trials, hearings, and depositions
docs.x: Mississippi land mine. Pro hac vice: local counsel must attend trials, hearings, and depositions: Mississippi local counsel cannot be a name on the pleadings only. Local counsel must personally attend every trial and, unless excused, every hearing, pretrial conference, and deposition in the state. Local counsel is also jointly and severally responsible. Papers you file before the pro hac vice order is lodged with the Supreme Court Clerk are struck. (M.R.A.P. 46(b)(4), (b)(7), (b)(11))

docs.t: Mississippi — Interlocutory appeal: 21 days, straight to the Supreme Court, no trial-court certification
docs.x: Mississippi land mine. Interlocutory appeal: 21 days, straight to the Supreme Court, no trial-court certification: Petition the Supreme Court within 21 days after the order is entered, and serve the trial judge and all parties. Unlike 28 U.S.C. § 1292(b), no trial-court certification is needed. The petition is limited to 15 pages including the brief, and no reply is allowed. The comment condemns seeking belated reconsideration to restart the 21 days. A petition does not stay trial-court proceedings unless ordered. (M.R.A.P. 5(a)–(c), (f) & cmt.)

docs.t: Mississippi — Certiorari from the Court of Appeals requires a rehearing motion first
docs.x: Mississippi land mine. Certiorari from the Court of Appeals requires a rehearing motion first: To reach the Supreme Court after a Court of Appeals decision, first move for rehearing in the Court of Appeals within 14 days. Then petition for certiorari within 14 days after the ruling on rehearing. The petition is limited to 10 pages, and the opinion and rehearing motion must be attached. Silence for 90 days after the response deadline is a denial. (M.R.A.P. 17(b), (e), 40(a))

docs.t: Mississippi anti-SLAPP — No anti-SLAPP statute; every 2022–2026 bill died in committee
docs.x: Mississippi anti-SLAPP. No anti-SLAPP statute; every 2022–2026 bill died in committee: Mississippi has no anti-SLAPP law. The Legislature’s official Bill Status System lists every measure by session. Its lists for the 2018–2026 regular sessions and the 2025 and 2026 extraordinary sessions show anti-SLAPP bills only in 2022, 2025, and 2026, and each one died in committee: • 2022: S.B. 2628 (Public Speech Protection Act). • 2025: H.B. 1504 (“Freedom of Speech Protection Act”). • 2026: H.B. 1268 and S.B. 2734 (Uniform Public Expression Protection Act), S.B. 2381 (Uniform Public Expression Act), and H.B. 1476 (“Freedom of Speech Protection Act”). The 2026 bills would have created the Act from scratch, which confirms none was already in force. There is no special motion to dismiss, no automatic discovery stay, no fee-shifting, and no interlocutory appeal for speech-based claims. Defendants us

docs.t: Mississippi anti-SLAPP — What the failed 2026 bills would have done (not law)
docs.x: Mississippi anti-SLAPP. What the failed 2026 bills would have done (not law): H.B. 1268, the Mississippi Uniform Public Expression Protection Act, would have applied to claims based on: communications in government proceedings; communications on issues under consideration in those proceedings; and the exercise of speech, press, assembly, petition, or association rights on a matter of public concern. It excluded claims by and against governmental units, provided an appeal, and would have applied to actions filed on or after July 1, 2026. It died in the House Judiciary A Committee on Feb. 3, 2026. Watch for a reintroduced version in the 2027 session. (2026 H.B. 1268 §§ 1–3 (as introduced))

docs.t: Mississippi anti-SLAPP — Related rule that does exist: notice before suing a newspaper or broadcaster for libel
docs.x: Mississippi anti-SLAPP. Related rule that does exist: notice before suing a newspaper or broadcaster for libel: Before suing a newspaper, radio station, or television station for libel, the plaintiff must give the defendant written notice at least 10 days in advance, identifying the article or broadcast and the statements claimed to be false. If the defendant acted in good faith on an honest mistake of fact and published a full and fair correction and retraction within 10 days after the notice, the plaintiff recovers only actual damages. The defendant must plead and prove these facts as affirmative defenses. The rule does not apply to editorials, opinion columns, or statements about a candidate made within 10 days of an election. docs.t: Mississippi appeal deadline — Notice of appeal (civil)
docs.x: Mississippi appellate deadline. Notice of appeal (civil): 30 days from Entry of the judgment or order (M.R.A.P. 4(a)). Filed with the trial-court clerk. Mandatory dismissal if late; the appellate courts cannot extend it in civil cases (M.R.A.P. 2(a)(1), 2(c)).

docs.t: Mississippi appeal deadline — Notice of appeal by another party / cross-appeal
docs.x: Mississippi appellate deadline. Notice of appeal by another party / cross-appeal: 14 days from Filing of the first notice of appeal (or the 30-day period, if later) (M.R.A.P. 4(c)).

docs.t: Mississippi appeal deadline — Tolling post-trial motions (M.R.C.P. 50(b), 52(b), 59; Rule 60 to toll)
docs.x: Mississippi appellate deadline. Tolling post-trial motions (M.R.C.P. 50(b), 52(b), 59; Rule 60 to toll): 10 days from Entry of judgment (M.R.C.P. 50(b), 52(b), 59(b), (e); M.R.A.P. 4(d)). Cannot be extended (M.R.C.P. 6(b)). Appeal time then runs from the order disposing of the last motion.

docs.t: Mississippi appeal deadline — Motion in trial court to extend appeal time
docs.x: Mississippi appellate deadline. Motion in trial court to extend appeal time: 30 days from Expiration of the original appeal time (M.R.A.P. 4(g)). Excusable neglect after expiration. Extension may not exceed 30 days past the original deadline or 10 days after the order, whichever is later.

docs.t: Mississippi appeal deadline — Motion to reopen appeal time (no notice of entry received)
docs.x: Mississippi appellate deadline. Motion to reopen appeal time (no notice of entry received): 180 days from Entry of judgment (or 7 days after receiving notice, if earlier) (M.R.A.P. 4(h)). If granted, the time is reopened for 14 days from the order.

docs.t: Mississippi appeal deadline — Designation of the record; cost deposit and certificate
docs.x: Mississippi appellate deadline. Designation of the record; cost deposit and certificate: 7 days from Filing of the notice of appeal (M.R.A.P. 10(b)(1), 11(b)(1)). Reporter estimate fallback: $300 per day of proceedings.

docs.t: Mississippi appeal deadline — Appellee’s additional designation
docs.x: Mississippi appellate deadline. Appellee’s additional designation: 14 days from Service of the appellant’s designation (M.R.A.P. 10(b)(4)).

docs.t: Mississippi appeal deadline — Court reporter files transcript
docs.x: Mississippi appellate deadline. Court reporter files transcript: 60 days from Service of the designation (M.R.A.P. 11(c)). One 30-day extension from the trial court; later extensions from the Supreme Court Clerk.

docs.t: Mississippi appeal deadline — Appellant’s brief
docs.x: Mississippi appellate deadline. Appellant’s brief: 40 days from Filing of the record (M.R.A.P. 31(b)). 50-page limit (M.R.A.P. 28(h)). Record excerpts filed at the same time (M.R.A.P. 30).
